# Rotate the Array by k — Explained, One Approach at a Time

<!-- Generated by scripts/gen-explained.mjs from src/data/problems/arrays-hashing/rotate-array.ts.
     Edit the data, then run `npm run docs:explained`. Edits here are overwritten. -->

**Arrays & Hashing** · medium · [the same question on LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/rotate-array/)

Given an integer array, move every value k positions to the right; the values that fall off the end wrap around to the front. The follow-up asks for it in place, with constant extra memory.

## What the input promises

- 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5
- -2^31 <= nums[i] <= 2^31 - 1
- 0 <= k <= 10^5, and k may exceed the length — k % n is the real rotation, so k = 7 on a 7-element array is no rotation at all
- the rotation is to the RIGHT: nums[i] ends up at index (i + k) % n
- in place: the follow-up rules out a second array the size of the input

## Examples

| Input | Output | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], k = 3` | `[5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4]` | — |
| `nums = [-1, -100, 3, 99], k = 2` | `[3, 99, -1, -100]` | — |
| `nums = [1, 2], k = 5` | `[2, 1]` | k is larger than the array. Without k % n every version below either loops five times for nothing or indexes past the end. |

<details>
<summary>Hints, one nudge at a time — open them in order</summary>

1. Rotating by n leaves the array exactly as it was, so only k % n matters. Reduce k before you touch a single value.
2. After the rotation the array is two blocks that swapped places: the last k values, then the first n - k.
3. Reversing the whole array puts both blocks on the correct side, each one backwards. Reverse each block to undo that.

</details>

---

## 1. One step at a time

Shift every value one place right, put the value that fell off the end at the front, and repeat that k times.

```python
def rotate_array(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    for _ in range(k % n):
        last = nums[n - 1]
        for i in range(n - 1, 0, -1):
            nums[i] = nums[i - 1]
        nums[0] = last
    return nums
```

**O(n * k) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] rotateArray(int[] nums, int k) {
    int n = nums.length;
    for (int step = 0; step < k % n; step++) {
        int last = nums[n - 1];
        for (int i = n - 1; i > 0; i--) nums[i] = nums[i - 1];
        nums[0] = last;
    }
    return nums;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
vector<int> rotateArray(vector<int> nums, int k) {
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    for (int step = 0; step < k % n; step++) {
        int last = nums[n - 1];
        for (int i = n - 1; i > 0; i--) nums[i] = nums[i - 1];
        nums[0] = last;
    }
    return nums;
}
```

</details>

## 2. Copy into a second array

> **Why now.** Shifting by one rewrites all n values k times over, which is 10^10 writes at the stated limits. The destination of a value never depended on the steps in between — (i + k) % n names it directly, so one pass places everything, at the cost of a full-size scratch array.

Every value's destination is known up front: nums[i] belongs at (i + k) % n. Write each one there in a new array, then copy that back.

```python
def rotate_array(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    moved = [0] * n
    for i in range(n):
        moved[(i + k) % n] = nums[i]
    for i in range(n):
        nums[i] = moved[i]
    return nums
```

**O(n) time · O(n) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] rotateArray(int[] nums, int k) {
    int n = nums.length;
    int[] moved = new int[n];
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) moved[(i + k) % n] = nums[i];
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) nums[i] = moved[i];
    return nums;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
vector<int> rotateArray(vector<int> nums, int k) {
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    vector<int> moved(n, 0);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) moved[(i + k) % n] = nums[i];
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) nums[i] = moved[i];
    return nums;
}
```

</details>

## 3. Cut and rejoin

> **Why now.** The formula version computes an index for every single element, and writing (i - k) % n by mistake rotates the wrong way — a bug that still passes on a palindrome. Naming the two blocks says what a rotation IS, so the direction is visible in the code instead of hidden in a modulo.

A rotation is two blocks swapping places. Take the last k values, put the first n - k after them, and that is the answer — two bulk copies, no per-element arithmetic.

```python
def rotate_array(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    k %= n
    nums[:] = nums[n - k:] + nums[: n - k]
    return nums
```

**O(n) time · O(n) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] rotateArray(int[] nums, int k) {
    int n = nums.length;
    k %= n;
    int[] out = new int[n];
    for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) out[i] = nums[n - k + i];
    for (int i = 0; i < n - k; i++) out[k + i] = nums[i];
    return out;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
vector<int> rotateArray(vector<int> nums, int k) {
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    k %= n;
    vector<int> out(nums.begin() + (n - k), nums.end());
    out.insert(out.end(), nums.begin(), nums.begin() + (n - k));
    return out;
}
```

</details>

## 4. Cyclic replacements

> **Why now.** Both copying versions allocate a second array as large as the input, which the follow-up forbids. Following the chain i -> (i + k) % n moves each value straight to its slot with only one value held aside — but the chain closes early when k and n share a factor, so it has to be restarted gcd(n, k) times.

Carry one value to its destination, pick up whatever was there, and carry that on. Each chain closes back where it started; start a new chain until all n values have moved.

```python
def rotate_array(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    k %= n
    moved = 0
    start = 0
    while moved < n:
        i = start
        carry = nums[start]
        while True:
            j = (i + k) % n
            nums[j], carry = carry, nums[j]
            i = j
            moved += 1
            if i == start:
                break
        start += 1
    return nums
```

**O(n) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] rotateArray(int[] nums, int k) {
    int n = nums.length;
    k %= n;
    int moved = 0;
    for (int start = 0; moved < n; start++) {
        int i = start;
        int carry = nums[start];
        do {
            int j = (i + k) % n;
            int t = nums[j];
            nums[j] = carry;
            carry = t;
            i = j;
            moved++;
        } while (i != start);
    }
    return nums;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
vector<int> rotateArray(vector<int> nums, int k) {
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    k %= n;
    int moved = 0;
    for (int start = 0; moved < n; start++) {
        int i = start;
        int carry = nums[start];
        do {
            int j = (i + k) % n;
            int t = nums[j];
            nums[j] = carry;
            carry = t;
            i = j;
            moved++;
        } while (i != start);
    }
    return nums;
}
```

</details>

## 5. The one to remember

> **Why now.** Cyclic replacements already run in place, but they need a count of how many values have moved (or a gcd) to know how many chains to start, and that bookkeeping is the part people get wrong. Three reversals reach the same arrangement with one primitive applied three times and nothing to count.

Reduce k to k % n, because a rotation by a multiple of n changes nothing. Then reverse the whole array: the last k values are now at the front and the first n - k at the back, which is the right arrangement of blocks with each block written backwards. Reverse the first k, then reverse the rest, and both blocks read forwards again. Three passes over the array with a swap loop, no allocation, and no index formula to get the direction wrong.

```python
def rotate_array(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    k %= n
    # whole array, then the two blocks the first reverse created
    for lo, hi in ((0, n - 1), (0, k - 1), (k, n - 1)):
        while lo < hi:
            nums[lo], nums[hi] = nums[hi], nums[lo]
            lo += 1
            hi -= 1
    return nums
```

**O(n) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] rotateArray(int[] nums, int k) {
    int n = nums.length;
    k %= n;
    for (int lo = 0, hi = n - 1; lo < hi; lo++, hi--) {
        int t = nums[lo]; nums[lo] = nums[hi]; nums[hi] = t;
    }
    for (int lo = 0, hi = k - 1; lo < hi; lo++, hi--) {
        int t = nums[lo]; nums[lo] = nums[hi]; nums[hi] = t;
    }
    for (int lo = k, hi = n - 1; lo < hi; lo++, hi--) {
        int t = nums[lo]; nums[lo] = nums[hi]; nums[hi] = t;
    }
    return nums;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
vector<int> rotateArray(vector<int> nums, int k) {
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    k %= n;
    for (int lo = 0, hi = n - 1; lo < hi; lo++, hi--) swap(nums[lo], nums[hi]);
    for (int lo = 0, hi = k - 1; lo < hi; lo++, hi--) swap(nums[lo], nums[hi]);
    for (int lo = k, hi = n - 1; lo < hi; lo++, hi--) swap(nums[lo], nums[hi]);
    return nums;
}
```

</details>

## The arc

| # | Approach | Cost | What it adds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | One step at a time | O(n * k) time · O(1) space | the baseline — nothing before it |
| 2 | Copy into a second array | O(n) time · O(n) space | Shifting by one rewrites all n values k times over, which is 10^10 writes at the stated limits. The destination of a value never depended on the steps in between — (i + k) % n names it directly, so one pass places everything, at the cost of a full-size scratch array. |
| 3 | Cut and rejoin | O(n) time · O(n) space | The formula version computes an index for every single element, and writing (i - k) % n by mistake rotates the wrong way — a bug that still passes on a palindrome. Naming the two blocks says what a rotation IS, so the direction is visible in the code instead of hidden in a modulo. |
| 4 | Cyclic replacements | O(n) time · O(1) space | Both copying versions allocate a second array as large as the input, which the follow-up forbids. Following the chain i -> (i + k) % n moves each value straight to its slot with only one value held aside — but the chain closes early when k and n share a factor, so it has to be restarted gcd(n, k) times. |
| 5 | The one to remember | O(n) time · O(1) space | Cyclic replacements already run in place, but they need a count of how many values have moved (or a gcd) to know how many chains to start, and that bookkeeping is the part people get wrong. Three reversals reach the same arrangement with one primitive applied three times and nothing to count. |

## Full runnable script

Every rung in one file, printed against the inputs `npm run verify:run`
drives the Java and C++ blocks with. Run it: `python explained.py`.

```python
def rotate_array_one_step_at_a_time(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    for _ in range(k % n):
        last = nums[n - 1]
        for i in range(n - 1, 0, -1):
            nums[i] = nums[i - 1]
        nums[0] = last
    return nums


def rotate_array_copy_into_a_second_array(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    moved = [0] * n
    for i in range(n):
        moved[(i + k) % n] = nums[i]
    for i in range(n):
        nums[i] = moved[i]
    return nums


def rotate_array_cut_and_rejoin(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    k %= n
    nums[:] = nums[n - k:] + nums[: n - k]
    return nums


def rotate_array_cyclic_replacements(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    k %= n
    moved = 0
    start = 0
    while moved < n:
        i = start
        carry = nums[start]
        while True:
            j = (i + k) % n
            nums[j], carry = carry, nums[j]
            i = j
            moved += 1
            if i == start:
                break
        start += 1
    return nums


def rotate_array_the_one_to_remember(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    k %= n
    # whole array, then the two blocks the first reverse created
    for lo, hi in ((0, n - 1), (0, k - 1), (k, n - 1)):
        while lo < hi:
            nums[lo], nums[hi] = nums[hi], nums[lo]
            lo += 1
            hi -= 1
    return nums

APPROACHES = [
    rotate_array_one_step_at_a_time,
    rotate_array_copy_into_a_second_array,
    rotate_array_cut_and_rejoin,
    rotate_array_cyclic_replacements,
    rotate_array_the_one_to_remember,
]

# the same inputs npm run verify:run drives the Java and C++ blocks with:
# reducing k before rotating — [1,2] with k=5 needs k % n, and [1,2,3] with k=3 must come back untouched
CASES = [
    lambda: ([1,2,3,4,5,6,7], 3),
    lambda: ([-1,-100,3,99], 2),
    lambda: ([1], 0),
    lambda: ([1,2], 5),
    lambda: ([1,2,3], 3),
    lambda: ([1,2,3,4,5,6], 4),
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for fn in APPROACHES:
        answers = []
        for make in CASES:
            try:
                answers.append(fn(*make()))
            except BaseException as exc:  # a rung that raises names itself
                answers.append(f"!{exc}")
        print(f"{fn.__name__:<39} -> {answers}")
```
